prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps), a far-term vision for air traffic management (ATM) in the National Airspace System (NAS). It interprets Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), is consistent with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept, and guides research. Far-term: NAS and most aircraft support Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2). Near- vs far-term: near-term is constrained by the current NAS and planned NAS Enterprise Architecture (EA)/NextGen changes and allows a limited TBO subset; far-term may assume future enablers and covers all air traffic control (ATC). Current NAS: automation predicts trajectories from flight plans; controllers issue open-trajectory tactical clearances; Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times to meet a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA); Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) trusts ETAs; Traffic Flow Management (TFM) leaves reroutes to controllers. MBT: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users negotiate closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) for all Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) aircraft; aircraft shall follow assigned 4DTs. NAS Constraint Service publishes NAS constraints to stakeholders and automation. Traffic management automation translates each traffic management initiative (TMI) into flight-specific trajectory constraints. Aircraft send predicted 4DT intent and updates. Conflicts are resolved by modifying 4DT constraints. Data comm delivers 4DTs to the Flight Management System (FMS); electronic flight bag (EFB) apps involve crew. Negotiating controller (subsumes D-side) coordinates with traffic management coordinators (TMCs). Time metric complements Performance Based Navigation (PBN), avoiding time of arrival control (TOAC). Near-term assumptions: controllers retain separation (no IFR self-separation, also far-term); equipage follows current standards; FMS Required Time of Arrival (RTA) limited to one active RTA; Controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) route clearances and trajectory intent output standard; gradual adoption amid mixed equipage; tools added via automation upgrades and System Wide Information Management (SWIM) extensions; uneven adoption, slow benefits until critical mass; user technology adoption at current pace. Actors: FAA, airspace users (commercial, UAS, space, on-demand), flight crew, controllers, TMCs, automation, NAS Constraint Service.

Document units:
U0067: Equipped aircraft from participating operators will benefit from the ability to negotiate their trajectories and will be more likely to be left alone to follow the assigned trajectory.  Current structured airspace will remain in use, although increased use of direct routing will be allowed in regions of low-to-medium operational density.  Controllers will use automation support to define and issue closed trajectories in advance, rather than reverting to open-trajectory vectors issued via voice. 1.5.2 Assumptions about the Far-Term MBT Environment  EFBs will become much more capable and will have reliable, high-speed connectivity to ground-based systems.
U0068: This will enable a rapid advance in air vehicle capabilities without requiring all of the changes to occur within legacy FMS architectures, which could be more expensive and slower to enter the fleet.  All aircraft will be capable of receiving assigned trajectories via digital communication and flying these trajectories with known accuracies.
U0069: Voice will continue to exist for cases when immediate feedback and action are required.
U0070: While many aircraft will be capable of digitally receiving trajectories and automatically loading them into the FMS, others will require pilots to manually load trajectory data into the FMS or otherwise fly the assigned trajectory.  The rapid advance of technologies and applications for unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) operations in the NAS will overflow into other categories of aviation operations.
U0071: Current Traffic Collision Avoidance System/Airborne Collision Avoidance System (TCAS/ACAS) technology will experience a substantial evolution based on emerging UAS detect and avoid capabilities.
U0072: This technology change will converge with technologies that support self-separation between aircraft (e.g., Advanced Interval Management [A-IM]).
U0073: As a result, the long-term environment will be characterized by all IFR aircraft being equipped with coordinated tactical conflict avoidance capabilities that can detect and safely avoid complex conflict scenarios involving multiple aircraft of all types, while providing the planned avoidance maneuvers to ground automation via broadband communication.
U0074: This will provide the final layer of safety in the MBT concept.  TFM will evolve considerably.
U0075: GDPs and AFPs will move toward controlling by CTA at the constrained NAS resource rather than departure time.
